newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-TYSON BACK IN STREET-TALKING FORM.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-TYSON BACK IN STREET-TALKING FORM.

text.p: Mike Tyson hasn't quite reverted to the days when he was the Sultan of Swill, but the heavyweight champion put his professed reverence for humanity on ice Thursday to trash-talk with pre-prison zeal.

Tyson, responding to brave talk and prodding from his co-managers, used a news conference announcing his November 9 fight against Evander Holyfield, to criticise his detractors with some vintage Tyson street language, including specific references to bodily functions.

The World Boxing Association heavyweight champion, who in the past has gone out of his way to profess newly-found peace and respect for humanity through Islam, also said nothing to defuse co-managers Rory Holloway and John Horne's threats that he would visciously punish Holyfield for disrespecting him.

The question is whether Holyfield said five years ago, after their original fight had been postponed and then Tyson was facing a trial for rape, that he would not fight a convicted rapist. Tyson spent three years in an Indiana prison after his conviction for raping a beauty pageant contestant.

"This is personal," Holloway said. "A lot of things were said about Mike Tyson during his trials and tribulations in the past by Holyfield ... He's got to pay the price. I'm going to be very eager to see the kind of pain he's gonna inflict on Holyfield."
Holyfield sat stoically on the dais in the Rainbow Room, 65 stories above Manhattan in Rockefeller Centre, while he was castigated by Horne and Holloway.
"No I didn't say that," said Holyfield, resplendent in a canary-yellow sport jacket and black t-shirt. "They can say what they want to pump him up. It don't make a difference. We still have to fight.
"This (criticising) is all being done for me. Why do they feel the need to do it?" Holyfield said.
"I didn't see him shouting at Bruce Seldon or Peter McNeeley," said Holyfield, referring to two of the easiest of four fights he has had since his release from prison.
But Tyson, who usually has been reticent in public since his release from prison in March, 1995, said: "I read the papers. He knows what he said. I know what he said.
"He should be a man to admit it. But like he said we still have to fight," said Tyson, wearing a cap turned backward on his head and a black t-shirt.
"He's a great fighter and all that," Tyson said, "but you're out of your league, man."

From most accounts of people close to the Tyson camp, the animosity between the two fighters who once were at least friendly toward each other, appears genuine and not aimed at selling the pay-per-view (ppv) fight, which is projected to gross well over $100 million to be the richest fight ever.

Tyson will receive a guaranteed $25 million and a cut of the ppv sales, and Holyfield has signed for about $12 million and a slice of the television sales, which Jay Larkin of Showtime Event Television says may come close to two million buys.

The price for the card, which also features an International Boxing Federation (IBF) heavyweight title fight between champion Michael Moorer and South African Francois Botha, will range from $45.95 to $49.95.
Botha was forced to surrender the WBC title earlier this year after testing positive for steroids. But the IBF still made him the number-one contender.
A third title fight -- a World Boxing Council bout between champion Ricardo Lopez of Mexico and an opponent to be named -- is also on the card.
Tyson is an 18-1 favourite to beat the former two-time heavyweight champion in their scheduled 12-round fight at the MGM Grand in Las Vegas.

Tyson won the WBC title by beating Frank Bruno last March, but under a court order he was forced to surrender it if he had not signed to fight Briton Lennox Lewis. Promoter Don King said Lewis had been offered $16 million to fight Tyson but turned it down.
